Executive Summary
As COVID-19 restrictions have eased and demand for passenger air travel has increased, airports have been facing issues with being short-staffed. A solution to this problem is to operate a robot that can perform important common airport tasks, such as flipping fuel levers, stamping passports, pressing boarding pass buttons, and depositing luggage. These robots can relieve staffing issues by performing these tasks in place of airport employees. Thus, a design competition was proposed by Brutus International Airport to the Institution Research and Development team to design and build a prototype for such a robot to be operated on a simulated airport course. Team A1 was one team participating in this design competition.
The team used a variety of methods throughout the process of designing and building the prototype robot. First, the team brainstormed ideas and design concepts. These ideas and concepts involved into a few preliminary sketches of possible designs. The team then came up with criteria to judge these possible designs and used these criteria and decision matrices to choose the best of the possible designs. From the best design, both a physical and CAD mockup were created. Building of the prototype began based on this mockup. Performance checkpoints were conducted weekly, testing the robot’s ability in successive weeks to navigate the course, press the boarding pass buttons, flip the fuel levers, stamp the passport, and deposit the luggage, respectively. Before each performance checkpoint, the team analyzed the tasks needing to be completed, designed a mechanism or method to perform the task, adapted the robot to incorporate the method or mechanism, tested the robot’s ability to perform the task, and made refinements, both mechanical and in code, as needed based on test results until the robot could consistently perform the required tasks. After all performance tests were passed and the robot could perform each task individually, the team compiled the code for each task into one unified program that could perform all tasks.
The final design of the robot consist of four 2.5-inch Dubro wheels driven by four Vex motors, a PVC floor, a 9.5-inch strip attached to a Futaba servo motor mounted at the rear of the robot with a Futaba box luggage container mounted at the end of the strip to stamp the passport and deposit the luggage, a Futaba box mounted at the front to press the boarding pass buttons, a fuel arm mounted to a Futaba servo motor at the front left to flip the fuel levers, and a CdS cell with a red filter mounted on the underside of the floor to detect light colors. The strengths of the design are its speed due to its unique four-motor design, its purpose-built fuel arm, and its long passport arm. Some weaknesses include its inconsistency due to hard-coded paths, the unfixed wheels, and the robot sometimes struggling to identify lights. Still, this final design could perform all the tasks required on the model airport course, addressing the mentioned design problem. Implementing a full-sized version of this final design can perform common airport tasks and help with airport staffing issues.
Future work could be done to improve many aspects of the robot design. The relatively flimsy PVC chassis could be strengthened with structural support or reinforcement. Different methods of navigation around the course, such as utilizing bump switches or line following could be used to improve the consistency of the robot. The wheels, which are not fixed to the robot in the team’s final design and can fall off when handled, could be mounted with increased security. Instead of cardboard, a luggage container could be built with a stronger material to improve stability of the container and consistency of depositing the luggage. Overall, the robot’s performance and consistency could be improved with further work and effort in design, building, and testing.

Introduction
	As the COVID-19 pandemic has eased, passenger demand for air travel has steadily increased. At the same time, airports have been short staffed; thus, the need for robots that can perform common airport tasks has arisen. Brutus International Airport has been exploring the incorporation of such robots and has tasked the Instution State Research and Development team to choose a prototype robot. Team A1 is one of the companies developing a prototype robot, which is to be tested on a robot course built by the Institution State Research and Development team. The purpose of building the robot was to develop a prototype for a successful robot that completes the necessary common airport tasks and can be implemented by Brutus International Airport to improve its operational efficiency. Team A1 consists of David Lee, Michael Smith, Rohan Sharma, and Vikram Patel. The final class robot performance test will be on 12 April 2024, while the showcase will be on 20 April 2024. 
	The sections of this report start off with the preliminary concepts and ideas where ideas for drivetrain analysis, code representation, and project constraints are included. Then, an analysis section is included with a discussion of successive tests and refinements. The report follows with the final design section, including the final robot design, code, and analysis. The class performance test section follows where the details, outcomes, analysis, and decisions of the class performance test are discussed. To finish, the summary and conclusion section summarizes the final project and provides takeaways for the future.
Preliminary Concepts and Ideas
Competition Requirements
	For the Engineering Honors Robot Competition, Team A1’s project had to adhere to certain criteria. Specifically, there was a $160 cost constraint to be utilized at the Academic Program Company store, the maximum robot size was 9 inches wide, 9 inches long, and 12 inches tall, robot testing was only available at limited times, and teams were limited to one Proteus microcontroller with limited motor ports. The robot had to perform the following tasks: start/end a run based on a light on the course, press the start button at the beginning of a run, flip the correct fuel lever, deposit the luggage in the appropriate area, press the correct boarding pass button based on a light on the course, raise a passport mechanism to stamp a passport, and come back to the start and press the start/end button to end the run. The time limit on a run was two minutes [1]. 
Initial Design Process
	Initially, the team individually brainstormed ideas for the mechanisms and drivetrain of the robot that is intended to accomplish the tasks laid out on the course. Each member of the team was able to visualize their ideas and communicate them with other members of the team. Throughout this process, the team was able to collaborate and offer more unified ideas of the drivetrain and mechanisms that the team intended to use. After ideas were fully developed for each aspect of the robot, a decision matrix was utilized for each aspect of the robot to rank the ideas and determine which were the best. These decision matrices can be found in the appendix from Table A1 through Table A6. Combining some of the best ideas from the results of the decision matrices, three possible designs emerged: 
	A four-wheeler with four powered wheels, a tall and narrow chassis, a fixed arm with a clamp on the end for pressing the boarding pass button, flipping the fuel levers, stamping the passport, and pressing the final button, and a tilting rectangular platform for luggage. 
	A 4-wheeler with treads, a platform chassis that bumps into the boarding pass button, stamps the passport, and presses the final button and raises, lowers, and tilts for depositing the luggage and flipping the fuel levers. 
	A four-wheeler with two powered wheels, a tall and narrow chassis, a rectangular surface that juts out which tilts to press the boarding pass button, deposit the luggage, and press the final button, a clamping arm for flipping the fuel levers and stamping passports. 
These designs are shown below in Figure 1, Figure 2, and Figure 3, respectively. Figure 4 shows a CAD mockup of the chosen robot design.
 
Figure 1: Preliminary sketch of design with four powered wheels.

 
Figure 2: Preliminary sketch of tread design.
 
Figure 3: Preliminary sketch of design with two powered wheels.
Lastly, the team compiled the ideas and criteria and utilized another decision matrix, which weighed each important element of the robot with the unified ideas discussed by the team, to choose to continue with the idea shown in Figure 1 with four powered wheels. The matrix is shown below in Table 1, below. With this decision made, both a CAD model and physical model, shown below in Figure 4 and Figure 5, respectively, were created.
Table 1: Decision matrix for initial robot design.
	Criteria (Weight)
Idea	Consistency of Success (5)	Speed (4)	Maneuverability (5)	Ease of Building (3)	Durability (2)	Low-cost (3)	Total
Idea 1	5	4	5	2	4	3	89
Idea 2	4	3	4	3	3	3	76
Idea 3	4	4	3	4	4	4	83

 
Figure 4: CAD mockup of chosen robot design.
 
Figure 5: Physical mockup of initial robot design.
Code Design
Preliminary ideas were also made for the code design. The team decided to utilize user-created functions to improve code efficiency and readability, including important functions to drive straight, turn, and rotate the arms and luggage platform. The main body of the function would then consist of calling these functions in the order in which they must be performed. A representation of the overall code in the form of an algorithm is shown in Table 2, below. 
Table 2: Algorithm created to represent overall code.
Step	Action
1	Wait for light to turn on or until 10 seconds has passed to move on to step 2
2	Move forward a few inches
3	Turn robot 45 degrees counter-clockwise
4	Get signal for fuel lever
4a	Case 1:  Go forward distance to first fuel lever
4b	Case 2:  Go forward distance to second fuel lever
4c	Case 3: Go forward distance to third fuel lever
5	Use mechanism to lift up fuel lever
6	Move forward until end of the yellow line parallel to fuel levers
7	Turn 90 degrees clockwise
8	Go forward until robot is on the ramp
9	Dump luggage into luggage collector
10	Line follow the white line
11	Move forward 1 inch
12	Get light color
12a	Case Red: Turn clockwise until parallel to the boarding pass buttons and move forward until inline with red button. Push button and then adjust to middle of boarding pass to push white button.
12b	Case Blue: Turn clockwise until parallel to the boarding pass buttons and move forward until inline with blue button. Push button and then adjust to middle of boarding pass to push white button.
13	Move backwards 7 inches
14	Turn 90 degrees clockwise
15	Move forward 6 inches
16	Turn 90 degrees clockwise
17	Lift passport up
18	Lift passport down
19	Move backward until robot goes down the ramp and is on lower floor.
20	Move backwards until robot hits finish button

Analysis, Testing, and Refinements
	Building Process and Decisions
The mock-up was very helpful in developing the initial build. While developing the mockup, it was found that the walls that were put for structural support did not provide much benefit to robot performance while increasing costs and mass. Therefore, the robot’s floor was first built, and the team would decide if further structures, such as emulating the walls of the mockup, were necessary if their need became apparent in the future. Also, it was found that using a vertical moving lever was not necessary and simply just attaching the arm to the servo motor was just as effective. The team decided to spread the wheels out more for more structural support as it caused problems in the mock-up. In spite of this, the mock-up still guided the team toward the general shape and design of the robot.
The floor, measuring 6 inches wide and 7 inches long, was cut from a piece of PVC. The next step was the attach the four motors. To figure out which motors were used, a drivetrain analysis was conducted. Sample calculations for each step are included in Appendix B. First, the distance the robot will travel in the course was measured and came out to 186.5 in. The time to accomplish each task was estimated with a small buffer and came out to 40 seconds. The minimum linear speed was calculated to be 2.35 in/s after accounting for margin of error using the following equation.
	s=  d/t	(1)

	Then, using a circumference of 2.5π, the rotational speed was found to be rounded to 18.0 RPM using the following equation.
	ω=s/C_wheel 	(2)

	Another part of the drivetrain analysis was the calculations for required torque. Using CAD, the mass of the robot was found to be 116.7 ounces. The angle of the steepest ramp on the course was measured to be 19.44 degrees. Using the following equation and an assumption of 8 ounces of internal friction, a required force of 46.84 ozf was found for the robot to go up the ramp.
	F=W sin⁡θ+f	(3)

	Then, a required torque of 58.55 ozf-in was found using the following equation and the wheel radius of 1.5 inches. This value equates to 14.64 ozf-in per motor for the four-motor design.
	τ=F*r_wheel	(4)

After obtaining the required RPM of 18.0 and required torque of 14.64 ozf-in, a torque versus speed graph of the available motors was consulted. The required thresholds were graphed, as seen below in Figure 6; all motors met our required speed and torque. Since all motors could work, Team A1 decided to utilize four Vex motors to maximize performance while being cost-effective—the Vex motors were considered to have the best price-to performance.  
 
Figure 6: DC motor torque-speed curves and the required thresholds for the chosen design [2].
	Results from Explorations
From the first exploration, the team was informed as to how to use the shop and the tools in it; this allowed the team to drill holes in the floor to mount the motors. After four Vex motors were mounted to the floor using brackets, screws, and nuts and four wheels were attached to the motors using two-inch axles, verification of the design began. The Proteus was attached to the floor using Velcro, and the motors were plugged into the Proteus. Verification of the design consisted primarily of ensuring that the motors worked, the robot could move forwards, backwards, and turn, and the robot could drive perfectly straight as desired. From the second exploration, the team learned how to implement a CdS cell and discovered that the red filter was best for distinguishing between red and blue light. Thus, a CdS cell with a red filter was mounted on the bottom of the robot, wired to the Proteus, and tested by placing it on red and blue light and reading the CdS values. Once the CdS cell values were confirmed, the robot could be easily triggered to start by the red start light in the code. From the third exploration, the team learned that line following was an effective method of navigating about the course while shaft encoding was an unreliable and inconsistent method of navigating around the course. The team thus decided against implementing costly shaft encoding while keeping in mind that implementing line following could be a good investment.
Results from Performance Checkpoints
To test the build of the robot, performance checkpoints were conducted weekly. The first robot performance checkpoint required the robot to move up the ramp and touch the boarding pass kiosk and come back down the other ramp. During the performance test, the path was coded in pieces; refinements were made to the path in the code after every test conducted in preparation for the checkpoint. Although the team was able to successfully complete the checkpoint, a problem the robot encountered was the inconsistency based on the battery level. To resolve this issue in the future, the team made sure that the battery level was high anytime the robot was being tested. Other than that, no mechanical refinements were required before the next checkpoint. A picture of the robot’s design after the first performance checkpoint is shown in Figure 7, below.
 
Figure 7: Robot's design after first performance checkpoint. 
	The second robot performance checkpoint required the robot to read a light using a CdS cell and press the respective boarding pass kiosk button. Again, although the team was able to successfully complete the task, the CdS cell had trouble correctly identifying the correct light. To resolve this, the team retaped the filter over the CdS cell to ensure that they weren’t conflicting with each other. During the performance tests, refinements were continuously made in the code to improve the path going to the boarding pass light and the threshold values for red and blue for more consistent results. After each test in preparation for the performance test, revisions were made in the code. The robot after the second performance test is pictured in Figure 8, below.
 
Figure 8: Robot after second performance checkpoint.
	The third robot performance checkpoint required the robot to flip the fuel levers, with extra points for flipping the correct fuel lever and keeping it down for more than five seconds. The team prepared for this performance checkpoint by 3D printing an arm to flip the fuel lever that could be attached to a Futaba servo motor. The arm and servo were then mounted onto the robot using superglue, and RCS functionality was added to the code to get the correct fuel lever from the system. The arm and servo motor worked extremely well. After continuous refinements to the code and successive testing were performed to get the robot to the correct positions, the arm consistently flipped the lever, kept them down for five seconds, and returned them to their original positions. As a result, the team passed the checkpoint and obtained all bonuses. The robot’s design following this checkpoint is shown in Figure 9, below (Proteus and wheel detached).
 
Figure 9: Robot after the third performance checkpoint with Proteus and wheels detached.
The fourth robot performance checkpoint required the robot to stamp the passport by lifting the passport mechanism, with extra points for lowering the mechanism back after stamping the passport. The team prepared for this performance checkpoint by designing a mechanism that could perform this task.  The team initially tried using the existing fuel lever from the third performance checkpoint to flip the lever; however, the team quickly realized this was not possible. So, the team decided to attach a 9.5-inch metal strip to another Futaba motor with one screw at the servo’s center of rotation. The motor was mounted using superglue at the rear of the robot so that the strip could rotate from left to right. After continuous refinements were made to the code after successive tests were performed, the robot reached the correct position, with the strip under the passport mechanism. However, the strip did not rotate with the servo. To solve this problem, a refinement was made to the design: another screw was added connecting the servo motor to the preexisting Futaba “arm.” After this refinement and several refinements in the servo angle so that the passport mechanism would be flipped enough to stamp the passport but not enough for the mechanism to not return back down, the robot successfully completed the task and the checkpoint, including the bonus for returning the mechanism back down. A picture of the robot after this performance is not available; however, the robot’s design at this stage was identical to after the fifth performance checkpoint, shown in Figure 10, with the exception that there was no Futaba box mounted on the rear servo and passport strip.
The fifth performance checkpoint required the robot to deposit the luggage, with extra points for depositing it in the higher area. The team prepared for this performance checkpoint by designing a container for the luggage to be carried in and deposited from. After some brainstorming, the team decided to attach a Futaba motor box to the end of the passport strip. This solution as seen to be cost-effective, as the box was already available to the team, and versatile, as the box could be mounted at any position. The team mounted the box onto the strip; after testing revealed that the mechanism no longer could complete the passport task, the team refined the design by mounting the box further away from the ground. After continuous refinements were made to the code after successive tests were performed in order to drive the robot to the correct position to deposit the luggage and to drive it back to press the final button, the design consistently deposited the luggage in the higher depository. The robot thus completed this checkpoint with the bonus and with an extra bonus for completing one class early. The robot after the fifth performance checkpoint is shown in Figure 10, below.
 
Figure 10: Picture of robot after fifth performance checkpoint.
Final Design
	Specifications
The final design of the robot carried two mechanisms and the traditional four-motor drivetrain that team A1 had been utilizing for the performance checkpoints. The first mechanism is the 3D-printed arm that is utilized to flip the fuel levers and click the buttons required in various tasks. The second mechanism is a long bracket with a rectangular platform at its end operated by the Futaba Servo motor, working to flip the passport and drop the suitcase for each respective task. Team A1 continued to use the four Vex motors as the primary drivetrain which is helpful for the robot to grip the ramps on the course and operate at faster speeds, allowing for higher efficiency. The final design of the robot is shown below in Figure 11.
 
Figure 11: Picture of robot's final design.
Code
The final code of team A1’s robot project has various functions that reduce repetition of code and simplify it for users and readers. These two functions are the turn(char direction, float time, int dominant_motor_percent, int nondom_motor_percent) taking in four arguments, and driveForward(float time, int percent) taking in two. The robot uses a combination of these functions to navigate to each task and these are necessary to ensure a consistent course path. Team A1 takes advantage of the four motors on the drivetrain in the turn() and driveForward() functions as the robot can independently control the percentage of each motor, allowing for precise turns and movement. Additionally, team A1 optimized the final code such that each performance checkpoint has a corresponding method with it, allowing for efficient error-handling and improved user-readability. These functions are all called in the main method of the code in the order that Team A1 intends the robot to complete the respective tasks. Also, this allows the team to easily change the order of the path if need be and lets team A1 to troubleshoot specific tasks. The complete code can be found in Appendix D. 
Strengths and Weaknesses
The final design has many strengths. The 4-wheel drivetrain offers increased traction on the steeper surfaces and power which allows for better speed. Our final fuel lever arm design is quick and effective at switching the fuel levers up and down in successive order. The longer arm raises the stamp the perfect amount so that it stamps the passport and then returns to its original position, therefore increasing efficiency. 
There are a few concerns with the final design. The axles that connect the 4 wheels to their respective VEX motors become loose with usage and makes the wheels prone to falling off when handling. The wheels themselves are not fixed to the motor—they usually operate without issue during the run but are prone to falling off when the robot is manually moved or worked on. Additionally, the hard coding of the path and many of the tasks resulted in inconsistency issues, especially as the battery level of the Proteus varied. The CdS cell also struggled with consistency in detecting the boarding pass light.
Budget and Time
For the overall budget, out of the original $160, $44.71 was left. A total of $115.29 was spent on the robot. A large portion of the budget was spent on motors. $60 was spent on the 4 VEX motors and $20 was spent on the Futaba motors. The rest of the budget was spent on PVC for the base, axles, mechanisms, and nuts/bolts/washers.
Everyone in the group spent at a minimum 6 hours working on the robot during class per week. Generally, Monday was spent on project management, documentation, and some construction. Wednesdays focused more on construction and code development with some testing towards the end of class. And finally, Fridays were generally only code development and testing so that whatever performance checkpoint that was on the docket would be completed successfully. Some time was spent outside of class depending on if some documentation wasn’t finished in class and this averaged out to 1-3 hours per week per person. Overall, 7-10 hours were spent per week per team member on all aspects of this robot project.
Class Performance Test
	Background
The class performance test was conducted on Friday, April 12 at the normal class time in Main Hall 101. It consisted of three runs for each team in the class to complete the entire obstacle course in one path. For the first run, all task requirements were randomized, and the test was performed on course C. For the second run, all task requirements were chosen by the Academic Program staff, and teams could find out about these requirements only upon arrival on the course. This run was completed on course D. For the third run, all task requirements could be chosen by the teams themselves, and the run was completed on course A. The course only permitted teams for performance test runs and only teams that are performing or on deck were allowed to stay in MH 101. Teams had two minutes upon being called to the course to arrive at the course and a further one minute to have the robot ready to start pending one “final action.” If the team was not ready after minute, a false start was declared— only one false start was permitted per run.

Results and Analysis
For the first run, Team A1 scored 0 points. The robot was unable to detect the starting light, inhibiting the robot from starting and hitting the red start button. This was quite peculiar as this was the first instance the team ran into this problem. At first, the team thought that this was due to improper electrical wire connection. This is because after unplugging the CdS cell wire and replugging it, the robot was able to detect the flashlight from an iPhone. However, this turned out to not be the case because the robot ran into the same problem in the third run, scoring 0 points, even though the team made sure the CdS cell was wired correctly. The most probable source of this problem was that a VEX motor wire blocked the CdS cell and since the starting light isn’t bright relative to a flashlight, the robot didn’t detect it. A potential solution to this issue that will be implemented for the robot competition is to have the robot wait around 8 seconds and back into the light in case the robot cannot detect the starting light.
However, for the second run, the robot was able to start and scored 26 primary points and 0 secondary points. The robot wasn’t precise enough and did not get to the correct position to flip the A1 fuel lever, so 0 points were gained. The next task was the luggage drop off and even though the robot got to the right spot, the servo motor for the mechanism was not strong enough for the luggage to fall out of the mechanism so 0 points were gained. The next task was the boarding pass button. The robot was able to detect the blue light for the task but wasn’t precise enough to hit the blue boarding pass button so 0 points were gained. The last task was the passport, and the robot was able to flip it up gaining 26 primary points. The robot was unable to hit the end course button so no more points were gained.
Summary and Conclusions
To start off the report, the introduction section provides a foundation of the goal of the project. Then, this report covered the team’s preliminary concepts and ideas for the robot and described the drivetrain analysis, code representation, and project constraints. After, an analysis section followed with a discussion of various performance tests and how the robot was improved upon after each one. Then, a final design section was included that describes the final state of the robot and its code after the refinements. 
Strengths of the robot include the control and speed of the design. Although it was expensive, the four-motor design gave this robot an edge over the others as it allowed the robot to move faster. Also, having four motors made the robot have more structured turns since each wheel can be controlled by the proteus.
Weaknesses of the robot include the CdS cell and the consistency of the path. Since a significant portion of the project went toward the four-motor drivetrain and the two servo motors, the robot had to rely on hard coding instead of sensors as it traversed through the path. This meant that line following and bump switches were not utilized causing inconsistencies in the robot’s path. Also, some problems arose with the CdS cell. Although, the CdS cell was able to consistently detect the starting light, there were instances where it would detect the wrong light for the boarding pass. This was likely caused by the weak structure that held the CdS cell in place.
Overall, this project proved to be a very iterative process. For example, even if the code appeared to correct, there were several factors that could affect the outcome of the trial run. All components of the robot had to be always analyzed and slowly iterated upon. Additionally, a lot was learned from everyone involved on how to be an effective teammate. There were a lot of deliverables to be acted upon, and communication on who was going to work on what was a very important key to success.
Many aspects of the robot could be improved upon in future work. The PVC chassis could be strengthened, adding structural support or reinforcing the material—it is currently rather flimsy. Bump switches and line following could be implemented to improve navigation ease and consistency around the course. The wheels could be attached in a better way that always fixes them to the robot, such as with shaft collars. A luggage platform with more stability could be built and attached to the robot. Overall, with more time, design work, and effort, the robot’s performance and consistency could be vastly improved.

#include <AcademicProgramUtility.h>

#include <AcademicProgramBattery.h>

// Servo Max: 2277
// Servo Min: 500

// servo2 max: 2330
// servo2 min: 500

// function prototypes for all functions
void driveForward(float time, int percent);
void turn(char direction, float time, int dominant_motor_percent, int nondom_motor_percent);
void fuel(int correctLever);
void luggage();
void boardPass();
void passport();
void driveback();

// declare motor on motor port 0, set maximum voltage to 9.0 V
AcademicProgramMotor blm(AcademicProgramMotor::Motor1, 7.0);
AcademicProgramMotor brm(AcademicProgramMotor::Motor3, 7.0);
AcademicProgramMotor flm(AcademicProgramMotor::Motor0, 7.0);
AcademicProgramMotor frm(AcademicProgramMotor::Motor2, 7.0);

// declare servo motors, s1 = fuel servo, s2 = passport/luggage servo
AcademicProgramServo s1(AcademicProgramServo::Servo6);
AcademicProgramServo s2(AcademicProgramServo::Servo7);

// declare CdS cell
AnalogInputPin light(AcademicProgramIO::P2_7);

int main()
{
    // initialize RCS connection
    RCS.InitializeTouchMenu("A1bXYZx99");

    // wait for start light to turn on
    while (light.Value() > 0.9)
        ;

    // Get correct lever from the RCS
    int correctLever = RCS.GetCorrectLever();

    // reset servo motors
    s1.SetDegree(180);
    s2.SetDegree(80);

    // Hit Starting light
    driveForward(0.25, -40);

    // call fuel function, passing in correct lever
    fuel(correctLever);

    // reset servo after fuel task
    s1.SetDegree(180);

    // intermediate step to turn to luggage task
    turn('R', 0.655, 100, -100);

    // call luggage function
    luggage();

    // intermediate step to turn towards boarding pass light
    turn('L', 0.81, 100, -100);

    // call boarding pass function
    boardPass();

    // call passport stamp function
    passport();

    // call drive back function
    driveback();
}

void fuel(int correctLever)
{
    // set arm so it doesn't hit an fuel levers
    s1.SetDegree(120);

    // drive towards levers
    driveForward(0.78, 100);

    Sleep(0.25);

    // slight left
    turn('L', 0.9, 100, 25);

    // Check which lever to flip and perform some action
    if (correctLever == 0)
    {
        // Perform actions to flip left lever
        
        driveForward(0.26, -100);

        Sleep(0.5);
        // flip down
        s1.SetDegree(100);
        Sleep(5.0);
        // flip up
        s1.SetDegree(135);

        Sleep(0.5);
        //reset arm
        s1.SetDegree(120);

        driveForward(0.84, 100);
    }
    else if (correctLever == 1)
    {

        // horziontally towards ramp
        driveForward(0.0625, 100);

        Sleep(0.5);
        // flip down
        s1.SetDegree(100);

        Sleep(5.0);
        // flip up
        s1.SetDegree(135);

        Sleep(0.5);
        // reset arm
        s1.SetDegree(120);

        driveForward(0.5175, 100);
    }
    else if (correctLever == 2)
    {
        // horziontally towards ramp
        driveForward(0.33, 100);

        Sleep(0.5);
        // flip down
        s1.SetDegree(100);

        Sleep(5.0);
        // flip up
        s1.SetDegree(135);

        Sleep(0.5);

        driveForward(0.25, 100);
    }
}
void luggage()
{
    // up ramp
    driveForward(1.9, 100);

    // turn right after ramp
    turn('R', 0.7, 100, -100);

    // drive to be aside luggage depository
    driveForward(0.7, 100);

    Sleep(0.6);
    
    // deposit luggage
    s2.SetDegree(30);

    Sleep(0.6);
}
void boardPass()
{
    // declare variables
    int button;
    int override;

    frm.SetPercent(40);
    flm.SetPercent(40);
    brm.SetPercent(40);
    blm.SetPercent(40);

    float t = TimeNow();

    //drive until light is detected, or if no light is detected, for 4.5 seconds
    while (light.Value() > 1.9)
        if (TimeNow() - t > 4.5)
        {
            override = 1;
            break;
        };

    frm.SetPercent(0);
    flm.SetPercent(0);
    brm.SetPercent(0);
    blm.SetPercent(0);

    // repositioning if robot missed light
    if (override == 1)
    {
        driveForward(0.5, -100);
    };

    // display light color and value on Proteus
    if (light.Value() < 0.9)
    {
        LCD.SetBackgroundColor(RED);
        LCD.Write(light.Value());
        LCD.Clear();
        frm.SetPercent(0);
        flm.SetPercent(0);
        brm.SetPercent(0);
        blm.SetPercent(0);

        button = 0;
    }
    else
    {
    LCD.SetBackgroundColor(BLUE);
    LCD.Write(light.Value());

    LCD.Clear();
    frm.SetPercent(0);
    flm.SetPercent(0);
    brm.SetPercent(0);
    blm.SetPercent(0);

    button = 1;
    }

    Sleep(0.5);

    LCD.WriteLine(button);

    // code to hit the correct button
    if (button == 0)
    {
        LCD.WriteLine("RED");
        driveForward(0.4, -100);
        turn('R', 0.54, 100, -100);
        driveForward(0.63, 100);
        turn('L', 0.41, 100, -100);
        driveForward(0.5, 100);
    }
    else
    {
        LCD.WriteLine("BLUE");
        driveForward(0.4, -100);
        turn('R', 0.54, 100, -100);
        driveForward(0.23, 100);
        turn('L', 0.41, 100, -100);
        driveForward(0.5, 100);
    }

    // code to back up from the button
    driveForward(0.2, -100);

    // turn robot rear towards passport mechanism
    turn('L', 0.8, 100, -100);

    // move passport servo all the way left to ground
    s2.SetDegree(150);
    Sleep(0.5);

    // drive towards passport mechanism
    if (button == 0)
    {
        driveForward(0.5, -100);
    }
    else
    {
        driveForward(1, -100);
    }
}
void passport()
{
    driveForward(0.22, 50);
    // flip passport mechanism up
    s2.SetDegree(60);
    Sleep(0.5);
    // servo back to ground
    s2.SetDegree(150);
    Sleep(0.5);
}

void driveback()
{
    // path to drive from platform back to start area
    turn('R', 0.8, 100, -100);
    driveForward(0.15, -50);
    s2.SetDegree(80);
    Sleep(0.5);
    turn('R', 1.0, -80, -25);
    driveForward(1.2, -100);
    turn('L', 1.0, -80, -25);
    driveForward(1.0, -100);
    turn('L', 0.7, -80, -25);
    driveForward(0.3, -100);
    turn('R', 0.7, -80, -25);
    // press final button
    driveForward(0.5, -100);
}

// function to drive forward
void driveForward(float time, int percent)
{
    // set all motors at desired percent
    frm.SetPercent(percent);
    flm.SetPercent(percent);
    brm.SetPercent(percent);
    blm.SetPercent(percent);
    // sleep for desired time
    Sleep(time);
    frm.SetPercent(0);
    flm.SetPercent(0);
    brm.SetPercent(0);
    blm.SetPercent(0);
}

void turn(char direction, float time, int dominant_motor_percent, int nondom_motor_percent)
{

    // set motors to desired percent based on desired direction
    if (direction == 'L')
    {
        frm.SetPercent(dominant_motor_percent);
        flm.SetPercent(nondom_motor_percent);
        brm.SetPercent(dominant_motor_percent);
        blm.SetPercent(nondom_motor_percent);
    }
    else if (direction == 'R')
    {
        frm.SetPercent(nondom_motor_percent);
        flm.SetPercent(dominant_motor_percent);
        brm.SetPercent(nondom_motor_percent);
        blm.SetPercent(dominant_motor_percent);
    }
    // sleep for desired time
    Sleep(time);
    frm.SetPercent(0);
    flm.SetPercent(0);
    brm.SetPercent(0);
    blm.SetPercent(0);
}

Based on the provided final report, here are the key moments where a navigation-related decision was made, changed, or dropped, along with an assessment of the justification versus the underlying reasons.

### Key Navigation Decisions, Changes, and Abandonments

#### 1. Initial Decision: Adopt a Hard-Coded Path
- **The Decision:** The team decided to navigate the course using a pre-programmed, hard-coded sequence of movements (forward, backward, turns) defined by time and motor percentages. This is detailed in the algorithm in Table 2 and the description of the first performance checkpoint.
- **Justification Offered:** The report does not explicitly justify this choice in the initial stages. It is presented as the default, straightforward method to execute the required tasks in order.
- **Assessment:** The offered justification is essentially "it was the simplest way to start." The surrounding context points to the underlying reason being **simplicity and pragmatism**. As a starting point for a complex project, a hard-coded path allowed the team to focus on building and testing individual mechanisms (like the fuel arm and passport stamper) without the added complexity of sensor integration and real-time feedback. It provided a baseline to measure progress against.

#### 2. Change: Reject Shaft Encoding for Navigation
- **The Decision:** During the third exploration, the team decided against using shaft encoders to track wheel rotations for navigation.
- **Justification Offered:** The report states that shaft encoding was found to be "unreliable and inconsistent" during testing. It was also deemed "costly."
- **Assessment:** The justification offered was likely the **primary cause** for this change. The team's own experimental results validated the unreliability of the method. The cost constraint ($160) would also make an additional component like shaft encoders a significant consideration. The context strongly supports that this was a practical decision based on empirical evidence from their own trials.

#### 3. Change: Consider Line Following as an Alternative
- **The Decision:** Also during the third exploration, the team identified line following as an "effective method of navigating about the course" and decided it "could be a good investment."
- **Justification Offered:** The justification was that line following worked effectively in their explorations, unlike shaft encoding. It was framed as a superior alternative worth considering.
- **Assessment:** The justification aligns well with the context. The team was looking for a more robust and consistent navigation method than their hard-coded path, which was already showing inconsistencies (e.g., based on battery level). Seeing line following work effectively provided a clear candidate for improvement. The underlying reason was the **recognition of a weakness in their current hard-coded approach** and the desire to build a more autonomous and reliable robot.

#### 4. Drop: Abandon Line Following and Bump Switches in the Final Design
- **The Decision:** Despite identifying line following as a potentially good investment, the team ultimately abandoned the idea and stuck with the hard-coded path for the final design. They also did not implement bump switches. This is explicitly stated as a weakness in the "Strengths and Weaknesses" and "Summary and Conclusions" sections.
- **Justification Offered:** The summary states that the team "had to rely on hard coding instead of sensors as it traversed through the path" because "a significant portion of the project went toward the four-motor drivetrain and the two servo motors." The implication is that resources (time, focus, budget) were allocated elsewhere.
- **Assessment:** The offered justification (resource allocation) is likely the **primary underlying reason**, but the context suggests a more nuanced story. The team was clearly aware of the benefits of line following but failed to implement it. The phrase "had to rely" implies a constraint-driven decision, possibly due to:
    - **Time Constraints:** Weekly performance checkpoints forced the team to focus on passing immediate tests, leaving little time for a major architectural overhaul like integrating line following.
    - **Complexity:** Integrating a new navigation system on top of the existing complex mechanisms might have seemed daunting.
    - **Prioritization:** The report highlights the time spent on the four-motor drivetrain and servo-operated mechanisms. It's plausible that the team prioritized perfecting these visible, task-specific parts over the less tangible navigation system.

In essence, the team justified the abandonment of advanced navigation by pointing to resource diversion, but the context of the iterative, checkpoint-driven process suggests that momentum and the difficulty of changing course mid-project were also significant, unstated factors. The final report's admission that this was a weakness and a point for future work confirms that they later viewed this as a missed opportunity.

So this response concludes that the team's resource constraints were a significant factor in abandoning line-following, driven largely by the decision to invest heavily in the four-motor drivetrain.
